strings.name: James Marape
strings.role: Prime Minister of Papua New Guinea
strings.summary: James Marape has been Papua New Guinea’s prime minister since 2019, after serving as education minister and finance minister. He advocates greater domestic returns from mining and energy development, alongside security cooperation with the United States and Australia and relations with China. His government also faces electoral controversies, public-security problems and pressure on public services.
strings.coverageNote: Sources checked through 18 November 2026, including his 17 November meeting with Xi Jinping in Shenzhen. The chronology distinguishes parliamentary selection of a prime minister from a direct popular vote, treaty signature from entry into force, and mine recommissioning from actual gold production.
strings.influence.rationale: His role in Papua New Guinea’s resource governance and international security cooperation, and his policies toward the United States, Australia and China, influence Pacific geopolitics.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and education
strings.facts.f1.value: Born on 24 April 1971 and from the Huli community. He graduated from the University of Papua New Guinea with a Bachelor of Arts in 1993. His education and highland-community background are important parts of his political career.
strings.facts.f2.label: Ministerial experience
strings.facts.f2.value: Education minister from 2008 to 2011 and finance minister from 2012 to 2019. After serving in Peter O’Neill’s government, he resigned from cabinet in April 2019, subsequently participating in a coalition realignment and joining PANGU.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Resource returns and national participation
strings.highlights.h1.text: He pursued renegotiated mining arrangements to increase Papua New Guinean interests. New Porgera’s 51% domestic stake is held collectively by national, Enga provincial and landowner stakeholders, not by him personally or the central government alone. Better returns must be assessed alongside shutdown costs, actual production and local distribution.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Governance and social pressures
strings.highlights.h2.text: The 2022 election involved violence, delayed counting and procedural disputes. Riots followed police protests over pay in January 2024, prompting a two-week state of emergency; the government attributed the pay changes to an administrative error. Security, employment, prices and public services remain central pressures in assessments of his government.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Meets Xi Jinping in Shenzhen
strings.timeline.t1.text: Met China’s president during travel connected with the APEC leaders’ meeting to discuss trade, investment and infrastructure cooperation. Reuters also reported his remarks about domestic resistance to closing Taiwan’s office. Taiwan had attributed the closure to Beijing’s pressure; these positions are presented as the respective parties’ accounts.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Signs the PNG–Australia Mutual Defence Treaty
strings.timeline.t2.text: Signed the Pukpuk Treaty with Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, elevating bilateral relations to an alliance. Australia’s official legal notice and the leaders’ statement confirm entry into force on 8 July 2026; the October 2025 signature was a separate milestone.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Witnesses New Porgera’s first gold pour
strings.timeline.t3.text: Attended the first gold-production event after the mine’s restart. Barrick had announced the beginning of recommissioning on 22 December 2023; the first-pour event followed in February 2024. Papua New Guinean stakeholders’ combined 51% ownership and production progress are different measures.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Government signs defence cooperation agreement with the US
strings.timeline.t4.text: Papua New Guinea’s government and the United States signed a defence cooperation agreement in Port Moresby to advance bilateral security cooperation. The US treaty record gives 16 August 2023 as its entry into force, distinct from the signature date.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Parliament elects him prime minister again
strings.timeline.t5.text: The first parliamentary sitting after the election took place while counting remained unfinished in some electorates. He was elected unopposed with unanimous support from MPs present. PANGU formed a coalition after winning the most seats; he did not take office through a direct popular vote or a single-party absolute majority.
strings.timeline.t6.title: First elected prime minister
strings.timeline.t6.text: The National Parliament elected him by 101 votes to eight after O’Neill resigned. His earlier departure from government contributed to the political realignment. On taking office, he proposed scrutiny of resource laws and project agreements; those pledges were not already-realized returns.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Becomes finance minister
strings.timeline.t7.text: Joined O’Neill’s government after the election to oversee finance, serving until 2019. Debates over public finances and resource revenues became important to his political career. This Finance portfolio is distinct from the Treasury portfolio he later also held.
strings.timeline.t8.title: First enters the National Parliament
strings.timeline.t8.text: Won election for Tari-Pori as a National Alliance candidate, later participating in the People’s National Congress and PANGU. Hela province was separated from Southern Highlands in 2012; its later boundaries should not be projected back onto his first election.
